summary: Provides a framework for handling Unicode strings in protocol slots such as usernames and identifiers. It defines how to prepare, enforce rules on and compare them so equivalent-looking strings are treated consistently. It was replaced by RFC 8264.

plainLanguage.summary: Words can look alike but be spelled differently in computer terms. This gives rules so computers agree two names match.

questions: what is the difference between identifierclass and freeformclass
subtitle: A framework for deciding which Unicode characters a protocol string may contain and how two such strings are compared.

tldr.problem: Protocols that carry Unicode text in usernames, identifiers and passwords need one consistent way to decide which characters are allowed and when two strings count as the same. The older Stringprep framework was tied to Unicode version 3.2.
tldr.mechanism: PRECIS defines two string classes, IdentifierClass and FreeformClass, built from Unicode character properties instead of fixed tables. Protocols add a profile that sets width mapping, case mapping, normalization and directionality, and rules are applied in a fixed order.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7564 obsoletes RFC 3454 (Stringprep) and has itself been obsoleted by RFC 8264.

today: RFC 7564 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 8264, so new work should follow the newer document. It obsoleted RFC 3454 (Stringprep).

sections.title: Why a New String Framework
sections.content:
Application protocols that carry Unicode characters in protocol slots such as addresses and identifiers must enforce internationalization rules and compare strings correctly, for example when making authentication or authorization decisions. RFC 7564 defines a framework for the preparation, enforcement and comparison of internationalized strings, abbreviated PRECIS.

Many IETF protocols had relied on the Stringprep framework in RFC 3454. After its publication in 2002, several issues arose with its use for internationalized domain names, most significantly that Stringprep was tied to Unicode version 3.2. The newer IDNA2008 specifications no longer use it. PRECIS is the post-Stringprep approach and is agile with respect to Unicode versions because it works from Unicode character properties.

The framework rests on four principles: a small set of string classes, classes defined by code point properties, an inclusion model in which anything not explicitly allowed is forbidden, and profiles that protocols may define but should not multiply beyond necessity.
sections.plainLanguage: The old rulebook for names was stuck on one old edition of the Unicode alphabet book. This new rulebook looks at what each character is like, so it keeps working when new characters are added.

sections.title: Preparation, Enforcement and Comparison
sections.content:
The RFC separates three actions an entity can take on a string.

  • Enforcement applies all rules of a string class or profile to one string, to decide whether it can be used in a protocol slot.
  • Comparison applies all the rules to two strings, to decide whether they are equivalent.
  • Preparation only checks that the characters in one string are allowed by the underlying string class.

In most cases authoritative entities such as servers enforce the rules, while subsidiary entities such as clients only prepare. Clients may lack the memory and processing power for rules such as width mapping and Unicode normalization, and a client cannot necessarily be trusted to generate such strings properly, especially for authentication and authorization.

The RFC also warns that turning an input string into an output string is rarely reversible. Case mapping turns StPeter into stpeter and the original capitalization is lost.
sections.plainLanguage: Checking a name is like a bouncer with a rulebook. A phone app only does a quick look at what you typed, while the server at the door does the full check and decides whether two names are the same person.

sections.title: The Two String Classes
sections.content:
The community concluded that most uses could be covered by two classes.

The IdentifierClass is a sequence of letters, numbers and some symbols used to identify or address a network entity such as a user account, a chatroom, a data feed or a file. Safety is prioritized over expressiveness. Valid code points are the traditional letters and digits (the LetterDigits category from RFC 5892) and the printable ASCII range U+0021 through U+007E. Spaces, symbols, punctuation, characters with compatibility equivalents and other letters and digits are disallowed.

The FreeformClass is for passwords and display elements such as nicknames. Expressiveness is prioritized over safety, so it allows nearly any Unicode character, including spaces, symbols, punctuation and characters with compatibility equivalents.

In both classes, the joining characters ZERO WIDTH JOINER (U+200D) and ZERO WIDTH NON-JOINER (U+200C) are allowed only when a contextual rule is met, and unassigned code points are treated as disallowed. Control characters, old Hangul Jamo and default-ignorable or noncharacter code points are disallowed in both.

The class of a code point comes from a derived property computed by an algorithm. Its steps must not be reordered, because that would give inconsistent results across implementations. Possible values include PVALID, CONTEXTJ, CONTEXTO, DISALLOWED and UNASSIGNED.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two kinds of name tags. The strict kind lets only plain letters and numbers, so nobody gets confused. The loose kind lets almost anything, even spaces and funny symbols, but it is easier to be tricked.

sections.title: Profiles and Their Rules
sections.content:
A profile of a string class MUST define five rules: width mapping, additional mappings (if any), case mapping, normalization and directionality. A profile MAY restrict the allowed characters further, but MUST NOT add as valid any code point that the class disallows. Profiles are registered with IANA under Expert Review.

  • Width mapping maps fullwidth and halfwidth characters to their decomposition mappings; for example FULLWIDTH DIGIT ZERO (U+FF10) becomes DIGIT ZERO (U+0030). It is generally RECOMMENDED when NFC is used.
  • Additional mapping covers things like delimiter characters or turning non-ASCII spaces into ASCII space.
  • Case mapping chooses case mapping or case preservation. If mapping is wanted, Unicode Default Case Folding is RECOMMENDED. For passwords it is NOT RECOMMENDED to map case.
  • Normalization picks a Unicode normalization form; NFC is RECOMMENDED.
  • Directionality handles right-to-left text. The framework defines no new directionality rule and suggests the Bidi Rule from RFC 5893 or the Unicode bidirectional algorithm instead.

The RFC says profiles must not be multiplied beyond necessity, because too many profiles lead to inconsistent behavior across applications and violate the Principle of Least Astonishment.
sections.plainLanguage: A profile is a set of house rules added on top of a name tag type: whether big and small letters count the same, how to write wide letters, and so on. The RFC begs people not to invent too many sets of house rules.

sections.title: Order of Operations and Using PRECIS
sections.content:
To get correct comparison, the rules of a string class or profile MUST be applied in a fixed order: width mapping, additional mapping, case mapping, normalization, directionality, and finally the behavioral rules that decide whether each code point is valid, contextual, disallowed or unassigned.

For application designers, the RFC advises not to define a new profile unless absolutely necessary, and to specify exactly which entities prepare, enforce and compare strings, when they must do so, and which protocol slots are checked against which profiles. An application may also exclude further code points for a slot, typically for backward compatibility. When a construct does not match a class, such as a SASL simple user name containing spaces, it can be built from several class instances, for example a space-separated sequence of IdentifierClass strings.
sections.plainLanguage: Cleaning a name always goes in the same order, like getting dressed: socks before shoes. If everyone does the steps in the same order, everyone ends up with the same result.

sections.title: Security and Confusable Characters
sections.content:
If strings that look the same are treated as different, or look different but are treated as the same, users get confused and security can suffer, for example through false positives in authentication or authorization (see RFC 6943).

The IdentifierClass is intended to be relatively safe, though it can still contain confusable characters. The FreeformClass can include virtually any Unicode character, so designers are encouraged to profile the IdentifierClass wherever feasible. The RFC gives an example of confusion even inside ASCII: ju1iet with the digit one can look like juliet. It states that PRECIS does nothing to map look-alike characters together and does not prohibit characters because they resemble others.

Services SHOULD define a policy on allowed scripts and SHOULD forbid strings that mix characters from more than one script. User-oriented software SHOULD warn when presenting mixed-script strings. For passwords, it is NOT RECOMMENDED to remove whole categories such as symbols or to map uppercase to lowercase; case should be preserved and compared case-sensitively.
sections.plainLanguage: Some letters look like other letters, like a number one and a lowercase L. Bad guys can use look-alikes to trick you, so the RFC tells services to keep their allowed letters few and to warn people about mixed-up names.
